sections.h2: How do you sell a house fast in Medina, Ohio?
sections.html:
A Medina owner can hire a broker, go it alone, or accept an offer that buys the house in its current state. Each version ends with a deed at the Medina County Auditor and a filing at the recorder.

Time and condition usually decide the choice. A listing can draw several offers, but it also brings showings, inspection findings and a contract tied to the buyer's loan. A cash purchase narrows the process to one conversation about price and closing date.

  • List with an agent: broader reach, plus commission and repair negotiations.
  • Go it alone: you set the price and run the process.
  • Sell for cash: one negotiated offer for the house in its current state.

sections.h2: How do Medina's Census numbers read for homeowners?
sections.html:
Medina's population is estimated at 25,692 on July 1, 2025, down 1.5 percent from a 2020 base of 26,075. Owner-occupied homes have a 2020-2024 median value of $243,600, and owners live in 67.3 percent of units.

Median gross rent is $1,077 and median household income is $77,385. Households number 10,911 at 2.33 people apiece, and 92.1 percent of residents stayed in the same home over the prior year. Of residents 25 and older, 35.6 percent hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

Land area is 11.58 square miles, so the 2020 count works out to 2,252.8 residents per square mile, and the grid around the Square is tight.

sections.h2: How does Medina's past show up in its houses?
sections.html:
Medina's center is a historic district, so older homes near the Square sit in a place that works to preserve its look. A Community Design Committee and a Historic Preservation Board look after the historic character, and the district covers a nine-block area around Uptown Park.

The Square dates to rebuilding after two fires. An 1848 blaze destroyed the whole business district, and an 1870 fire destroyed 45 buildings, after which it took almost ten years to replace the buildings, which is why the Victorian style is so common there.

sections.h2: Where is Medina, and which schools serve it?
sections.html:
Medina is about 33 miles south of Cleveland and 23 miles west of Akron, and the city has parts in Lafayette, Medina, Montville and York townships. Many residents commute to Cleveland and Akron, and RPM International is among the companies based in town. Workers spend a mean of 24.3 minutes getting to their jobs, per QuickFacts.

The Medina City School District serves the city. Its schools include Medina High School, A.I. Root and Claggett middle schools, and the elementary schools Ella Canavan, H.G. Blake, Sidney Fenn, Eliza Northrop and Ralph E. Waite. Garfield and Heritage elementary schools closed at the end of the 2023-24 school year after redistricting.

The Medina County Career Center serves 11th and 12th graders and adults, and the private options include St. Francis Xavier School and Medina Christian Academy.

sections.h2: What civic landmarks and local news serve Medina residents?
sections.html:
The Old Medina County Courthouse is among the city's landmarks, and the Medina County District Library has its main branch in town. Uptown Park anchors the center, and the nine-block historic district surrounds it.

The Medina County Gazette publishes every day except Sundays and federal holidays, and The Medina Post is a free weekly that comes out on Saturdays. Television and radio reach the city from the Cleveland, Akron and Canton markets.

The Medina County Career Center South Campus sits a quarter-mile south of the city and teaches adult courses in law enforcement, run with the Medina County Sheriff's Office, and in paramedic training.

sections.h2: What does Medina's Building Department regulate?
sections.html:
The city's Building Department handles plan review, inspections and property maintenance enforcement, and it tries to link owners of run-down properties with assistance programs and volunteer groups. You can reach it at 330-722-9030.

Ohio's 2024 Building, Mechanical and Plumbing Codes took effect March 1, 2024, and the department holds every application received after that date to those requirements. Ask the city's Planning Department any zoning questions about a lot or an outbuilding.

After a finished basement, a new deck or replaced mechanicals, ask the department whether the permits were closed out. A buyer's inspector will ask too, and a cash buyer will price any gap.

sections.h2: What does the Medina County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?
sections.html:
Medina County's real property conveyance fee is $3.00 for every $1,000 of sale price, per the auditor. The auditor rounds a price up to the next $100 when it ends in a fraction, and an online calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

The auditor's site separates taxable conveyances from exempt ones and posts a form for each. They include DTE 100 for value, DTE 100EX for exemptions and a statement for farm-use valuation land.

Ask the auditor how the current figure applies to your sale before you set a price.

sections.h2: Which Medina transfers are exempt from the conveyance fee?
sections.html:
The county lists more than two dozen exemption reasons, and several of them involve families and estates. Among them are transfers:

  • Gifts between spouses or between a parent and child.
  • To an heir or devisee, between spouses, to a surviving spouse, or on the death of a registered owner.
  • Transfers where nothing of value changes hands and no gift is involved.
  • To a trustee when the trust's grantor can revoke it freely.
  • Under a court order, to the extent the transfer is not a sale carried out under that order.
  • On sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.

An exempt transfer still needs paperwork. Ohio Revised Code 319.202 swaps the full value statement for a short statement of the exemption reason.

sections.h2: What happens if a Medina property is a rental?
sections.html:
A rental parcel needs a contact filing at the county auditor, with updates due 60 days after any change (Ohio Revised Code 5323.02). The auditor's endorsement on a rental deed points the new owner to that filing.

Mention the tenants and the lease in your first conversation with a buyer, and keep records of deposits and rent already paid.

sections.h2: When might a cash offer suit a Medina seller?
sections.html:
Cash tends to fit when the owner wants certainty more than the widest market. In Medina that can include owners with historic-district houses that need expensive work, heirs who live away, and landlords who want out of a rental.

  • Ask what is assumed: as-is, closing costs and move-out date.
  • Compare the figure to a listing net after repairs, commission and carrying costs.
  • Read the contract for who pays the conveyance fee and recording charges.

faqs.q: How much is the Medina County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Medina County Auditor states $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price. A sale price ending in a fraction of $100 is rounded up to the nearest $100, and the auditor offers an online calculator.

faqs.q: Does an inherited house in Medina owe the conveyance fee?
faqs.a: Usually not. The county exempts transfers to an heir or devisee and among heirs when no money is paid. The buyer or recipient still files the exemption statement, DTE 100EX.

faqs.q: Do I have to give a buyer Ohio's disclosure form?
faqs.a: Yes for houses of one to four units, subject to exceptions. A buyer who gets it after the contract is signed has three business days to rescind (Ohio Revised Code 5302.30).

faqs.q: Why does Medina Square have so many Victorian buildings?
faqs.a: The business district was destroyed by fire in 1848, and a second fire in 1870 destroyed 45 buildings. Rebuilding took almost ten years, and the Square is now a recognized historic district.

faqs.q: Where can I ask about building permits in Medina?
faqs.a: Call the city's Building Department at 330-722-9030. The department regulates construction and enforces property maintenance, and the Planning Department answers zoning questions.
